Documentation must describe what the product actually does right now, not what it used to do, might do, or is supposed to do. When a feature is removed, broken, or has no effect (e.g., an env var or config flag that silently does nothing), don't leave stale or softened language like "deprecated soon" or "has no effect in this release" — either remove the documentation entirely or fix the underlying product and document the working behavior. Documenting non-functional features looks inconsistent and misleads users into relying on them.

Before merging docs, verify every command, flag, and code sample actually works as written (e.g., confirm flag ordering like `cline connect telegram --restart -k <TOKEN>` truly works, not just that it looks plausible). When describing caveats or edge cases (such as "hooks don't run for providers that handle tool calls internally"), give users a practical way to recognize the situation themselves rather than an incomplete list of examples, and consider calling out caveats visually (e.g., a dedicated callout style) so they aren't missed. For reference tables describing evolving formats (e.g., CLI JSON event types), avoid claiming the list is exhaustive; instead instruct consumers to tolerate and skip unrecognized values for forward compatibility.

In short: remove or fix documentation for anything that no longer works, verify examples before publishing, and make caveats both honest and actionable.
